close_reason: Added Deviation.priority: i32 field (default 0). Updated DeviationStore::find_deviation and DeviationStore::find_deviation_for_chain to resolve by highest-priority-wins, with insertion order as the tie-breaker (matches the documented contract on both methods). The default priority of 0 preserves the prior 'first-match-wins-in-insertion-order' behavior for single-author stores; operators merging deviation files from multiple authors can now set explicit priorities to express specificity (site-local lab-scoped waivers get high priority, workspace-wide wildcard waivers stay at 0). Added Deviation::with_priority builder. The OSCAL Risk parser defaults priority to 0 on import; round-tripping priority through the OSCAL Risk extension model is a separate scope (left as a comment in parse.rs). Three regression tests: find_deviation_higher_priority_wins, find_deviation_priority_tie_breaks_by_insertion_order, find_deviation_negative_priority_loses_to_default. 268 lib tests + 7 doc tests + workspace tests pass; clippy --all-features --all-targets clean.
description: Site: deviation.rs:733-750. Doc says: 'In the case of multiple matching deviations, the first one added to the store wins. Deviations should be scoped to avoid unintentional overlap.' Scenario: operator merges two deviation files from two policy authors. Both target the same lint_id ('rfc5280.bc.ca_true_required' for an internal CA), one scoped 'any', one scoped 'issuer_dn_contains: internal-lab'. The 'any' deviation is added first (alphabetical merge by filename), so it wins for the lab CA cert too — but the lab-scoped deviation has a more specific justification and authorized_by. The lab-scoped deviation never fires. Maintenance consequence: when an auditor asks 'who authorized this waiver for cert X?', the answer is the 'any' deviation's authorized_by, not the lab-scoped deviation's. Wrong attribution in the audit trail. Fix: either (a) document and enforce a specific ordering rule (most-specific scope wins; or longest scope description wins; or explicit priority field on Deviation); (b) reject overlapping deviations at add time; (c) apply all matching deviations and surface the conflict to the operator. Option (a) with an explicit priority field is the most operator-friendly and matches how DACS/eBNF systems handle similar policy stacking. Pre-1.0 is the time to fix this — post-1.0 the on-disk OSCAL format gets harder to change.
title: DeviationStore::find_deviation 'first match wins' is order-dependent without ordering contract
